A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PoliCon benchmark. Their complete 45-page documents, including appendices, tables, equations, and figures, support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of six LLMs, evaluator agreement with parliamentary votes, and analyses of topic difficulty, party influence, and partisan bias.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds heuristic-baseline results, two human evaluation studies, and a seat-allocation robustness experiment.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction framework, two-stage evaluator, task objectives, and prompts are retained. Appendix C.3 newly specifies averaging the existing alignment and feasibility scores, without describing a change to the implemented procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 2,225 parliamentary records, 19 topics, and 15 task configurations forming 28,620 scenarios. The human checks and seat-resampling experiment examine existing coverage. Appendix A.6 explains previously undocumented filtering rather than establishing a changed dataset.

E2.justification: v3 adds Random and Greedy to the overall comparison in Table 1: they select a random party's stance or the largest party's stance, respectively. The six evaluated LLMs and topic-level comparator sets remain unchanged. v2's random-resolution bias control did not provide these benchmark comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 adds substantial validation protocols: 100 generated resolutions rated by 20 annotators, with three annotations per resolution; 100 cleaning samples assessed by ten annotators on a 0-5 scale; and 30 seat allocations per issue for four-party development/VP tasks. Existing LLM inference settings and benchmark metrics are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's historical-vote validation and qualitative cleaning example, v3 tests evaluator agreement with humans on generated resolutions and quantitatively assesses cleaning quality. Appendix F.2 also adds sensitivity analysis of VP outcomes to seat allocations. These address important evaluator, data-quality, and robustness questions.

E5.justification: Table 10 newly reports mean-plus/minus dispersion across 30 seat allocations, described in the text as mean and variance. The human agreement study introduces three independent annotations per item. Existing historical-vote error reporting is retained; Appendix E.1 additionally documents its standard-deviation and KDE calculations.

E6.justification: All existing LLM benchmark table values and figure results are retained. New results include Greedy's two-party SM score of 0.80, exceeding Qwen2.5-32B's retained 0.74; evaluator-human mean error of 1.61 in Table 2; cleaning ratings of at least 3/5 for over 95.8% of resolutions and over 75% of stances; and Table 10's repeated-allocation VP results. These substantially expand the evidence without establishing improvements in the original LLM scores.

T1.justification: The mathematical task definitions and voting conditions remain unchanged. Appendix E.1 supplies standard formulas for the existing error, standard-deviation, and density-visualization calculations, rather than new theoretical results or revised mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's four contributions, and conclusion retain the same benchmark scope, novelty claim, and principal findings about consensus difficulty and partisan behavior. Added validation supports these existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 interprets human agreement as evidence of evaluator generalization, adds the qualification that Greedy outperforms several LLMs in two-party voting tasks, and argues that seat sampling yields robust VP results. Existing mechanism explanations and the limitations discussion are retained.

D1.justification: v3 documents filtering criteria and counts reconciling 2,735 intermediate records with the retained 2,225, specifies averaging the two evaluator scores, and provides scipy KDE settings, bandwidth selection, and plotting resolution. It also documents annotation procedures and interfaces and explicitly announces code release through the existing project link. These are substantial reproducibility disclosures.

R1.justification: Scott (2015) is added to support KDE bandwidth selection. The related-work discussion, other cited works, and positioning relative to political benchmarks and deliberation research remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. v3 expands the validation narrative, adds experimental-details and LLM-usage appendices plus acknowledgments, and makes localized corrections, including changing 'under 60%' to 'over 60%' in the veto explanation while retaining its formal condition.

P2.justification: Conversion to the ICLR format changes typography, margins, headers, caption styling, display sizes, and placement throughout. Table 1 gains baseline rows, Tables 2 and 10 are added, and Figures 11-12 show annotation interfaces. Existing figures are retained and repositioned rather than redrawn.

improvement.justification: v2 supported evaluator validity through historical votes and cleaning quality through a qualitative example. v3 adds direct human validation of generated resolutions and cleaning quality, substantially strengthening evidence for two central benchmark components. Heuristic comparisons improve performance calibration, while filtering and score-aggregation disclosures resolve important reproducibility gaps. These gains outweigh the localized overstatement of robustness from the single-topic seat-allocation study; broader robustness remains unestablished.
